title: In the beginning was the Word (John 1:1–5)
hook: the light shines in darkness and the darkness did not comprehend it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last page of Luke: a blessing at Bethania, and disciples going home with great joy. Who got your blessing last night? Day four hundred ninety-two, and a new Gospel.

Matthew starts with a family tree. Mark starts with a man shouting in the desert. Luke starts with an old priest in the temple. John starts before anything started. No Bethlehem, no shepherds, no Jordan River. Just: in the beginning. If those words sound familiar, they should. They are the first words of the whole Bible, the opening of Genesis, before light, before land, before anyone. John borrows them on purpose. For the next six weeks we read the fourth Gospel in order, and on day one it reaches back past the first day of creation.
screen: `MATTHEW: A FAMILY TREE.` → `MARK: A VOICE IN THE DESERT.` → `JOHN: BEFORE ANYTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening, in the Douay-Rheims: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Today's word is the one John uses, logos. In Greek it means a word, but also reason, an account, the meaning behind things. Greek philosophers had used logos for the order running through the universe. Jewish readers knew of God's word that creates, and of Wisdom, who was with God at the making of the world. John takes all of that and says something none of them said: the Word was with God, and the Word was God. Then: "All things were made by him: and without him was made nothing that was made." Not a thing in your kitchen, not a star, not a cell, is outside him. And then, light: in him was life, and the life was the light of men. "And the light shineth in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it." Comprehend is a lovely double word. It can mean understand, and it can mean grasp, seize, get hold of. The darkness didn't understand the light, and it couldn't get hold of it either. Translators have argued for centuries which John meant; many think both. Saint Augustine remembered the old priest Simplicianus telling him that a Platonist philosopher used to say these opening lines deserved to be written in letters of gold and set up in every church. On Christmas Day the Church reads them at Mass, so that the baby in the manger is heard with this first: before Bethlehem, the Word.
screen: `IN THE BEGINNING, AGAIN.` · `LOGOS: WORD, REASON, MEANING.` · `ALL THINGS WERE MADE BY HIM.` · `THE DARKNESS DID NOT COMPREHEND IT.` · then, large: `AND THE WORD WAS GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a candle in the dark. If you can, turn off the lights and light a candle, or simply switch on one small lamp in a dark room, or picture it. Settle, and breathe. Watch the light. Notice that the dark doesn't push it out. Notice how far one small flame reaches. Let the words come back slowly: the light shineth in darkness. If you pray, you can rest in that line. If you don't, just stay with the flame and the dark around it. The bell holds the time.
Logos. Greek for word, reason, meaning. John's name for the one who was with God in the beginning, and who was God. Today's word.
Your line: the word was god. Today, when you turn on a light in a dark room, let it remind you of the first line of John. Day four hundred ninety-two.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Word means the Bible.
what it means: in John, the Word is a person, with God from the beginning, and God, through whom all things were made.
what a scholar hears: logos carries Greek ideas of reason and Jewish ideas of God's creating word and Wisdom; the verb in 1:5 (katalambanō) means both grasp and understand.
